opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, I think Ali was the right person from pretty early on, and that wasn't obvious to everyone at the time, including some of us. When we started Databricks, we were a group of researchers out of Berkeley, and a lot of us had the instinct that whoever had the deepest technical background should probably lead. Ali's strength was different. He's technical, he did his PhD in distributed systems, but what really stood out was that he was relentlessly focused on the business and on the customer in a way most academics aren't.

Early on, a lot of us thought the open source project would sort of sell itself. Spark was taking off, and we figured if we built a great product, people would come. Ali was the one who kept pushing on questions like: who's actually paying, what problem are they trying to solve, why would an enterprise trust a tiny startup with their data? He went out and talked to customers constantly, and he was willing to change his mind fast when the data said we were wrong.

The other thing is that he's very good at long-term thinking while still being demanding about execution in the short term. A lot of the big bets, like going all in on the cloud when many customers were still on-prem, or later the lakehouse idea, required conviction for years before they clearly paid off. He was willing to make those calls and then hold the team accountable for actually delivering.

And personally, it's been a really good split for me. I get to spend most of my time on technology, research, and product direction, and I trust him completely to run the company. That kind of trust among cofounders is rare, and I think it's a big part of why Databricks has worked as well as it has.

r001.rationale: The candidate says Ali talked with customers and changed his mind based on data, but does not describe him learning from experts he could not hire.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I'm obviously biased because I've known Ali for a long time—we overlapped at Berkeley, and we co-founded the company together—so take this with that caveat. But honestly, I think he's been an extraordinary fit for the role, and I'd say that even if I weren't involved.

A few things stand out to me. First, he actually understands the technology deeply. He came out of the same research environment, he was working on Spark and the surrounding projects, so when he's talking to engineers or making bets on where the platform should go, he's not operating from a slide deck. He can engage with the substance. That matters a lot in a company whose whole value proposition is technical.

Second, and this is maybe the thing people underrate, he's an incredibly fast learner on the business side. When we started, none of us had run a company before. We were a bunch of academics. Ali just absorbed everything—how enterprise sales works, how to structure a go-to-market team, how to think about pricing, how to work with a board—at a pace that was kind of remarkable to watch. He's very honest about what he doesn't know and he goes and fixes that.

Third, he's willing to make big, somewhat uncomfortable bets and then actually commit to them. The move toward the lakehouse framing, the push into SQL and data warehousing when a lot of people thought we should stay in our lane, the acquisitions in the AI space—those weren't obvious calls at the time, and there was internal debate. But he made decisions and got the organization aligned behind them.

And then there's just the stamina and consistency. Being CEO of a company at this scale for this long, through multiple market cycles, is grueling, and he's still as energized about the mission as he was in the early days. I think that comes through to the team.

So, yeah—I'd say he's been about as good a fit as you could hope for. The rest of us founders are pretty lucky he took that on.

r001.rationale: The response says Ali learned business skills quickly and addressed what he did not know, but it does not say he learned from experts when he could not hire them.

astra-6.text: I think Ali is a great fit for the CEO role. He combines technical depth with the ability to think about the business and build a strong team. For a company like Databricks, you need someone who can understand the technology but also connect it to what customers actually need. That combination is what makes him effective.
